# I. RATION CARDS [italic]Entry one. Day 203 since I left. Written at 0340, colony time.[/italic]
The few people here who know what I was ask me what the Union is like. They expect the posters. Red sky, gold star, a worker holding up a wrench like a sword. The posters were real. They were glued over the water damage in our corridor.
I grew up in a hab stack on a world that was full before I was born. Nine of us in two rooms. My mother's ration card was punched at the canteen every morning by a woman who never looked up. Protein bar, grain, tea that was mostly the colour of tea. On holidays, a tin of fish with the thanks of the Party printed on the lid. You learned not to complain about the fish. Someone always heard.
The embassy here says hardship shared is hardship halved. That is true. What they do not say is who does the sharing, and who checks the halves.
At eighteen they took me for the Naval Infantry. Our platoon was a whole Union in forty bunks: Spaniards like me, Russians, Germans, men from the old Chinese provinces who taught me to play cards for cigarettes. We were proud. We were also hungry. Boots came patched. Our rifles were copies of copies of something a corporation built, and the political officer told us that was a victory, because we had taken it from them.
He lectured every rest day. The corporatists are slaves who think they are free. The Americans want our worlds. Doubt is a wound the enemy makes. I nodded with the rest. I believed some of it. I still believe some of it, which is the worst part.
Nobody leaves the Union. Not because the door is locked. Because your family is still standing on the other side of it.
[color=#5A5040]-- I wrote my sister's name here. I deleted it. --[/color]
